paras: The arrest of Branch Payne was an exchange of gunfire in New Orleans on the night of August 16, 1900, between two deputy sheriffs and Payne, a Black man they had come to arrest, after which a crowd of "angry citizens" gathered and was dispersed by police. Payne submitted to arrest and was jailed under double guard, and no injuries were reported. A Chicago Tribune dispatch, reprinted across the country, presented the incident as "another outbreak against the negroes" narrowly averted in the neighborhood where Robert Charles had been killed weeks earlier.

According to the dispatch, Payne was "a powerful negro" who lived in the neighborhood where Robert Charles, whom the report called "the negro desperado," had been killed a few weeks before. The deputies carried a warrant charging Payne with shooting at a white man. The coverage gives no details of that earlier incident.

When the two deputy sheriffs tried to serve the warrant, the correspondent wrote, Payne "resisted arrest and shot at the officers, who returned the fire." Four shots were exchanged, and none was reported to have hit anyone. "Angry citizens quickly gathered," the report continued, but the police "charged the crowd in numbers and forced a dispersal."

Payne, described as "frightened by the demonstration," then submitted to arrest. He was placed in jail with double guards protecting him. The only account of the shooting is the correspondent's, which follows the officers' version; Payne's own account does not appear.
No report of a hearing, trial, or disposition of the charge against Payne was found in the coverage.

The story reached readers as a special to the Chicago Tribune from New Orleans, sent under a Chicago dateline of August 17. The Washington Evening Star ran it that day under "Race Riot Narrowly Averted" and "New Orleans Police Save a Negro From a Mob," crediting the police with preventing violence. The Providence News likewise praised "Prompt Action by New Orleans Police," though its headline added "He Tried Suicide," a claim its text does not mention.

Other editors cast Payne as the cause of the trouble. The Butte Daily Inter Mountain headed the same text "Another War in Prospect" and "Negro Desperado in New Orleans Starts a Riot," while the Waterbury Evening Democrat chose "Negro Trouble Again." The Deseret Evening News and, on August 18, the Portland Daily Press and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer framed it as race trouble, with headlines such as "Negro Outbreak Averted" and "Looked Like a Riot." The Morning Astorian went furthest, saying Payne "Was With Difficulty Rescued From a Mob."

A shortened version datelined New Orleans ran in weeklies through August 25 under "Fired on Deputies" and "New Orleans Negro Came Near Starting Trouble Afresh." All of these papers printed the same body text, and no report of the incident was found in the Black press or in a Louisiana paper.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune New Orleans correspondent (officers' version)
accounts.gist: Payne opened fire on two deputies serving a warrant, they returned fire, four shots were exchanged, a crowd gathered and was dispersed by police, and Payne then submitted and was jailed under double guard.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headed the Tribune special 'Race Riot Narrowly Averted' and 'New Orleans Police Save a Negro From a Mob,' crediting the police.
Other papers cast Payne as the cause, e.g. 'Negro Desperado in New Orleans Starts a Riot' (Butte) and 'New Orleans Negro Came Near Starting Trouble Afresh' (weeklies).
The Providence News added 'He Tried Suicide' to its headline, a claim absent from the body; the Morning Astorian said Payne was 'With Difficulty Rescued From a Mob.'

versions.value: Body text, identical in all copies, says nothing of a suicide attempt

conflicts.note: The Providence News headline is unsupported by its own text; it may be a headline error or belong to another item.

info: Night of August 16, 1900 ('last night' in a dispatch dated August 17)
New Orleans, in the neighborhood where Robert Charles had been killed a few weeks earlier
Branch Payne, described as 'a powerful negro'
Charged by warrant with shooting at a white man; also said to have fired on the deputies who came to arrest him
Two deputy sheriffs (exchange of shots); a crowd of 'angry citizens' gathered afterward
Crowd dispersed by police; Payne held in jail under double guard; no later report of the charge found
